My read of what is being suggested is that the level at which one should aim to understand and be comfortable with is slightly more abstract than reading the code and reviewing every line of it. It is like how one is comfortable not understanding the byte-level code or assembly language code. I know that this analogy doesn’t hold very well because compilation is a deterministic process while llms are not, but that is precisely the point being made. “Trust” that llm will produce the right output, even though the output might not be reproducible word for word the next time you give the same prompt.To your point about becoming redundant without understanding, not understanding things will be a problem when an issue arises and the other person isnt able to handle it the right way. However, if llm can address the issue, does the fact that they did not understand the details really matter? From the perspective of a person who gets to decide who gets fired, would they fire someone who is productive but sometimes introduces bugs that they quickly address or would they fire someone who is comparatively slow but rarely introduces bugs? Don't shoot the messenger, but maybe the idea is this:You're smart, and you know what can go wrong, so you use models slowly, and you check their work.  Your bet is that it will make a bad mistake.Your coworker is reckless, they don't know or care what can go wrong, so they use models quickly. title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs (e-means.github.io)
comments: I wonder if this could be used anywhere as an alternative to Lloyd's algorithm. I have a hobby project which uses Lloyd's to "relax" an icosohedral equal area mesh on the surface of a sphere [1]. I'm going to try to swap it out with an adaptation of this and see if it's much better or if I can afford more iterations with this method.Edit: tried it, and it’s definitely not better for this use case. e-means wins by needing fewer passes over a huge dataset, but relaxing a mesh on a sphere has no dataset: each Voronoi cell’s centroid can be computed directly from its geometry. Mini-batches just swap that for a noisy sampled estimate of the same thing. It has the same objective and the same optimum, so at best it matches Lloyd. In practice it was much slower and left the grid noisy, and with small sample budgets it even tangled the mesh.[1] https://webgcm.app/explain/grid#nudging-the-cells-into-shapereply

Since it's basically a linear interpolation between Lloyd's algorithm and not moving any points it will be at least as good but gains might be limited without careful tuning.Edit: in fact you might end up going faster by moving the other way, set alpha = -0.1 and see what happens!reply
I adapted the method to my IVF index (the code-daemon project) and achieved a 146x speedup on the GPU.That's impressive!reply

As far as I can tell this isn't particularly new, people have been doing minibatch k-means for a while, including with an EWA update. I assume the contribution here is that they tried to measure how much better it is and provided code? I'm not sure I agree with their claims though, because they didn't really measure the things that matter–sure, it's better than Lloyd's algorithm, but that's a very low bar.If you are claiming that your algorithm is "highly parallelizable" and comes with "wall-clock speedups", then the actual metrics that matter here is not number of steps or even basic wall clock time as your size remains fixed, but how your algorithm scales as more data is present or parallelism is required. This algorithm splits up the minibatch across workers and has them compute local updates, then allreduces it. As the amount of data goes up, the comms become much more expensive (since you have to use a worse transport layer), which means that you're basically locked in a desperate attempt to do more local work before you send your partial update to everyone else. If you attempt this (not explored in the paper) you will find that the improvement in clustering by doing this extra work has diminishing returns–you only reduce the number of updates by a few steps (which is what drives your wall clock time). At scale you end up being heavily comms limited and not super parallel at all.reply

These kinds of algorithms tend to have equivalent descriptions as expectation maximisation or simulated annealing. I wonder if it's possible to understand their algorithm in that sense.Though I suppose it may be as simple as expectation maximization with a friction term, since Sj = sj - a (sj - Sj).Importantly they note that this update rule keeps the centroid within the convex hull, which is pretty important.reply

comments: I didn't mention this in the article, but this isn't the first time my family has been driven almost spare by a mysterious, hard-to-track beep.Our dog goes outside and hides in the lavender bush if a smoke alarm starts making a "I need a battery" noise.So I went into this project with the attitude that I would like to solve this class of problem forever.reply

You can also solve this in O(logn) using a physical binary search:1) Move half the boxes to another room.2) Listen for a beep and determine which room the beep comes from.3) Take the boxes in that room and split them in half again.4) Repeat until one box is left.reply
It's O(logn) but you haven't accounted for how heavy each item in the array of n is.reply
If you randomly index them and there's enough of them then on average the partitions average out.reply
This is true, but it probably isn't a box of books that's beeping.I also feel like ordering the moves by lightest box first is reasonable as a real-world optimization.reply
Lol classic “ignore the constant factor” gotcha when using Big-O.reply
Or you could use a very heavy blanked to just cover some boxes to supress the sound enough to simulate moving boxes.reply

Yes, but that's also O(log n) physical effort. This one's O(1) sitting on your butt.(Out of curiosity: I think "physical binary search" is more properly O(n^{1/3} log(n)), or maybe O(n^{1/2} log(n)). Since physical objects have sizes, and moving things (or moving between things) takes time proportional to distance).reply

Good point about the moving effort required. But if moving an object takes constant time, then it's O(n) overall -- since <incorrect argument deleted>.EDIT: My earlier analysis was wrong (it assumed you never move the beeping item after the initial halving), but the conclusion was right for a different reason: Each time you move items, you move half as many as you did last time. You initially move n/2 items, and the geometric series n/2 + n/4 + n/8 + ... + 1 sums to n-1. So O(n) moves are done, and this dominates the log n term for the number of steps.reply

title: Horible public key tricks (maurycyz.com)
comments: xxx
first_paragraph:
So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS.
It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website.
Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing:
even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server.

... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections,
and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4"


There is prior art of protest SSL implementations,
but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic.
Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing:
therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate.

The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key.
Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes).

first_paragraph: AI agents wrote 613,318 lines of Lean that copy Python's internals line by line, tested every piece against the real Python, had a computer check every proof, and turned up 418 bug reports in Python along the way.Python doesn't have a precise written definition. There is a reference manual, but in practice "Python" means whatever CPython does, and CPython is hundreds of thousands of lines of C plus a large standard library. The manual covers normal use. It says little about the odd cases, and that's where bugs hide: an object that changes a dictionary while that dictionary is searching for it, an error thrown halfway through an update, a number one past the largest the C code was written for.Writing a proof about a function forces you to say exactly what it does in all of those cases. You can't leave anything vague, because the proof checker won't accept it. title: A primer on GPUs and kernel optimization (nabo.dev)
comments: Crazy to not see a word about benchmarking/evaluation of the kernels.IMO at this time when all performant GPU kernels are generated/hill-climbed, its the largest source of error we see.Should be kernel run with a hot or cold cache in practice? Should your kernel be bitwise equivalent to a ref? What error margins should your kernel have to ref? How many times are you running the kernel to avoid thermal noise? Are you running on separate GPUs to avoid overfitting the current hardware? Can you cudagraph-compiling your kernel to remove launch overhead? Are you A/B B/A interleaving your kernel/reference runs to avoid running thermal bias?reply

As someone who loves being able to press a button to receive matmuls tuned to the 3090 by his feet, are there rules of thumb to work out how to set thresholds for evals?Do I want to set a particular threshold on any individual op (or a layer for a given transformer)? e.g "for this test set, 99% of l2norms being within 1e-4 error of the golden reference kernel"Or do I want to just shortcut all that and go with task based evals? eg "word error no worse than 1% greater than the reference speech-to-text model"?I'm assuming the latter is the way to go in the first instance?reply

It depends on if you do training or inference and also at what scale.For your task with the 3090, and I assume inference, I would like you suggest do end-to-end on target task.Sometimes for example, a normalization layer can cancel out/fix an error from a previous layer, then it makes no sense to spend flops to save the numerics.This is kind of a wild west in inference serving, you sometimes change exp to tanh, sometimes go full 4bit, sometimes remove full layers because you still perform fine on the end-task.Numerics and correctness are more important for training kernels and backwards passesreply

Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost, Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see."Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic.When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Wo

title: Parking-app convenience fees in 312 U.S. cities (median $0.35 per session) (parkgraph.com)
comments: It shouldn't be called a "convenience fee" unless you can opt out of it and pay some other non-convenient way. What if I don't want their version of convenience? Why should I have to pay a convenience fee? Why can't they just roll this into the main price of parking? It's gotten to the point where as soon as I see the word "fee" I assume I'm being ripped off.reply

Why can't they just roll this into the main price of parking?Be careful what you ask for. A common ploy for dominating marketplaces (Amazon, Doordash, etc) is to prohibit merchants from offering lower direct prices than what's offered on their platforms. They always say this is to guarantee that you'll get the best prices with them. But that's a twisted way of saying all prices must be at least as high as theirs, and the point, of course, is to remove any incentive for merchants not to use the middleman.reply
Then wouldn't it make more sense to roll this into the main price so the main price seems higher rather than lower?reply

The common example is Mastercard and Visa. They charge a fee to the merchant but they require that that the merchant cannot offer you a lower price to pay some other way to avoid the fee. On top of that, there are 2 fees, one for "regular cards" and one for "premium cards" (gold cards, platinum cards). They charge the merchant more when a user uses a premium card but they require the merchant not to tell you.In an ideal world (well, my ideal world), these fees would be called out so that you, the customer, could choose not to pay them. You might see, "if I pay cash this $100 product will cost $100 but if pay with my platinum card it's $105. I can save $5 by paying cash".Mastercard and Visa forbid this for two reasons: (1) they don't want you choose the cheaper cash option (2) they don't want a competitor to be able to offer a lower fee. In the example above, they charge $5 but a competitor could charge $1. You'd might pick the cheaper option but you're unaware of it since they forbid the merchant from offering.They can only do this because they effectively have a duopoly on the market. Don't play by their rules, lose 99% of your customers. Various governments try to fix this. The cynical reason it hasn't been fixes is they pay off politicians to make sure it doesn't get fixed.reply
At least in my town you can opt out by paying with coins. So the convenience fee is for not having to carry coins around. For me at least it's worth the trade.reply

I find it weird that it's okay for a city to pay someone to come around to collect the coins, at no additional cost to the customer, but swiping/tapping? Absolutely not, that must be passed through to the customer.I'm sure for the city tap to pay is cheaper for them than collecting the $, even without a fee.reply
Cities have plenty of employees without much to do.Coins, being cash, are simple, require no apps, smartphones, batteries, tracking, ads, or privacy violations.reply
They should just call it what it is, a booking fee.Nothing inherently wrong with a booking fee if it is transparent.reply
How is that any different? It's still a fee you can't opt out of by using a different methodreply
The direct way to to pay at their kiosks but those often conveniently can never read your card or with lots of dollar coins and quarters.reply
